claim: Presynaptic active zones at the pillar IHC side activate at lower IHC potentials than those of the modiolar side.
source: Presynaptic active zones at the pillar IHC side activate at lower IHC potentials than those of the modiolar side that have more presynaptic Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known finding that provides context for the study.

claim: Modiolar side active zones have more presynaptic Ca2+ channels than pillar side active zones.
source: Presynaptic active zones at the pillar IHC side activate at lower IHC potentials than those of the modiolar side that have more presynaptic Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Postsynaptic SGNs differ in their spontaneous firing rates, sound thresholds, and operating ranges.
source: The postsynaptic SGNs differ in their spontaneous firing rates, sound thresholds, and operating ranges.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about SGN diversity.

claim: Synapses with high spontaneous rate of release were found predominantly on the pillar side of the IHC.
source: Synapses with high spontaneous rate of release (SR) were found predominantly on the pillar side of the IHC.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2I showing significantly higher SR for pillar synapses.

claim: High SR synapses had larger spontaneous EPSCs than low SR synapses.
source: These high SR synapses had larger and more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs, lower voltage thresholds, tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites, shorter response latencies, and higher initial release rates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2J showing significantly larger sEPSC amplitudes in high SR synapses.

claim: High SR synapses had more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs than low SR synapses.
source: These high SR synapses had larger and more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs, lower voltage thresholds, tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites, shorter response latencies, and higher initial release rates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2L showing higher percentages of monophasic sEPSCs in high SR synapses.

claim: High SR synapses had lower voltage thresholds than low SR synapses.
source: These high SR synapses had larger and more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs, lower voltage thresholds, tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites, shorter response latencies, and higher initial release rates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3Eii showing Q10 EPSC was significantly more hyperpolarized in high SR synapses.

claim: High SR synapses had tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites than low SR synapses.
source: These high SR synapses had larger and more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs, lower voltage thresholds, tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites, shorter response latencies, and higher initial release rates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3H showing significantly lower Ca2+ cooperativity in high SR synapses.

claim: High SR synapses had shorter response latencies than low SR synapses.
source: These high SR synapses had larger and more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs, lower voltage thresholds, tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites, shorter response latencies, and higher initial release rates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4B showing significantly shorter synaptic delays in high SR synapses.

claim: High SR synapses had higher initial release rates than low SR synapses.
source: These high SR synapses had larger and more temporally compact spontaneous EPSCs, lower voltage thresholds, tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and vesicular release sites, shorter response latencies, and higher initial release rates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4G showing significantly higher initial release rates in high SR synapses.

claim: Synaptic heterogeneity in IHCs directly contributes to the diversity of spontaneous and sound-evoked firing of SGNs.
source: This study indicates that synaptic heterogeneity in IHCs directly contributes to the diversity of spontaneous and sound-evoked firing of SGNs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: Paired recordings were performed on mice after the onset of hearing (postnatal days 14-20).
source: Simultaneous paired patch-clamp recordings from IHCs and one of the postsynaptic SGN boutons were performed on mice after the onset of hearing (postnatal days [p] 14–20).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental approach.

claim: IHCs were held at their presumed physiological resting potential of -58 mV.
source: We performed perforated-patch whole-cell configuration from IHCs, held at their presumed physiological resting potential (–58 mV; Johnson, 2015), and ruptured-patch whole-cell recordings from one of the postsynaptic SGN boutons (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and cites Johnson, 2015 as the source for this value.

claim: Recordings were made at body temperature.
source: Recordings were made at body temperature and in artificial perilymph-like solution (Wangemann and Schacht, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing experimental conditions.

claim: Recordings were made in artificial perilymph-like solution.
source: Recordings were made at body temperature and in artificial perilymph-like solution (Wangemann and Schacht, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Wangemann and Schacht, 1996.

claim: CaV1.3 Ca2+ channels activate at low voltages (−65 to –45 mV).
source: Since CaV1.3 Ca2+ channels activate at low voltages (−65 to –45 mV; Koschak et al., 2001; ; Picher et al., 2017a; Platzer et al., 2000; Xu and Lipscombe, 2001), their open probability at the IHC resting potential is thought to be sufficient to trigger spontaneous release (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002; Özçete and Moser, 2021; Robertson and Paki, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the voltage range.

claim: The open probability of CaV1.3 Ca2+ channels at the IHC resting potential is thought to be sufficient to trigger spontaneous release.
source: Since CaV1.3 Ca2+ channels activate at low voltages (−65 to –45 mV; Koschak et al., 2001; ; Picher et al., 2017a; Platzer et al., 2000; Xu and Lipscombe, 2001), their open probability at the IHC resting potential is thought to be sufficient to trigger spontaneous release (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002; Özçete and Moser, 2021; Robertson and Paki, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the inference about spontaneous release.

claim: Spontaneous EPSCs were observed in 23 of 33 pairs.
source: Under our experimental conditions, spontaneous, i.e., excitatory postsynaptic currents in the absence of IHC stimulation (sEPSCs) were observed in 23 of 33 pairs (Figure 1B, Figure 2, 20 recordings were targeted to the pillar side and 13 to the modiolar side).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: 20 recordings were targeted to the pillar side and 13 to the modiolar side.
source: Under our experimental conditions, spontaneous, i.e., excitatory postsynaptic currents in the absence of IHC stimulation (sEPSCs) were observed in 23 of 33 pairs (Figure 1B, Figure 2, 20 recordings were targeted to the pillar side and 13 to the modiolar side).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design.

claim: sEPSCs trigger SGN firing with >90% probability.
source: We used the rate of sEPSCs (SR) as a surrogate of SGN SR as sEPSCs trigger SGN firing with >90% probability (Rutherford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Rutherford et al., 2012.

claim: Estimated rates of sEPSC underestimate the SGN SR for the same age group.
source: Regardless of all efforts to maintain the physiological integrity in the ex vivo experiments, we expect our estimated rates of sEPSC to underestimate the SGN SR for the same age group (Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on citation to Wong et al., 2013.

claim: Amplitudes of sEPSCs typically varied from around –10 to –400 pA across all recorded IHC-SGN synapses.
source: Amplitudes of sEPSCs typically varied from around –10 to –400 pA across all recorded IHC-SGN synapses (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The amplitude histogram for all pairs was slightly skewed toward smaller amplitudes with a skewness of 1.06.
source: The amplitude histogram for all pairs was slightly skewed toward smaller amplitudes (skewness of 1.06) with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.68 (a similar distribution was obtained from 12 bouton-only recordings during which the IHC was not patched [Figure 2—figure supplement 1A]).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The amplitude histogram for all pairs had a coefficient of variation of 0.68.
source: The amplitude histogram for all pairs was slightly skewed toward smaller amplitudes (skewness of 1.06) with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.68 (a similar distribution was obtained from 12 bouton-only recordings during which the IHC was not patched [Figure 2—figure supplement 1A]).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The charge distribution for all pairs displayed a prominent peak at 40 fC.
source: The charge distribution for all pairs displayed a prominent peak at 40 fC, with a skewness of 2.00 and a CV of 0.77.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The charge distribution for all pairs had a skewness of 2.00 and a CV of 0.77.
source: The charge distribution for all pairs displayed a prominent peak at 40 fC, with a skewness of 2.00 and a CV of 0.77.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: SR ranged from 0 to about 18 sEPSC/s.
source: SR ranged from 0 to about 18 sEPSC/s (Figure 2H; a similar range of 0 to about 16 sEPSC/s was recorded without patch-clamping the IHC).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The SR distribution was highly skewed, with a median of 0.2 sEPSC/s.
source: The SR distribution was highly skewed, with a median of 0.2 sEPSC/s.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Approximately 70% of synapses were classified as low SR (<1 sEPSC/s).
source: Following the spontaneous firing rate classification of mouse SGNs by Taberner and Liberman, 2005, we classified the synapses into low (<1 sEPSC/s, ~70%) or high (≥1 sEPSC/s, ~30%) SR synapses (see Figure 2A for examples).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Taberner and Liberman, 2005.

claim: Approximately 30% of synapses were classified as high SR (≥1 sEPSC/s).
source: Following the spontaneous firing rate classification of mouse SGNs by Taberner and Liberman, 2005, we classified the synapses into low (<1 sEPSC/s, ~70%) or high (≥1 sEPSC/s, ~30%) SR synapses (see Figure 2A for examples).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Taberner and Liberman, 2005.

claim: Of the 33 obtained paired recordings, 20 were classified as pillar synapses.
source: Of the 33 obtained paired recordings, 20 were classified as pillar synapses.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The mean amplitude of sEPSCs was comparable between modiolar and pillar SGN boutons.
source: The mean amplitude (Figure 2C) and charge (Figure 2D) of the sEPSCs were comparable between modiolar and pillar SGN boutons (AmpsEPSC –69.37±13.91 pA [n=8 modiolar] vs –87.21±9.49 pA [n=15 pillar]; p=0.2913, unpaired t-test; QsEPSC 63.74±7.77 fC [modiolar] vs 72.54±9.57 fC [pillar]; p=0.5463, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mean charge of sEPSCs was comparable between modiolar and pillar SGN boutons.
source: The mean amplitude (Figure 2C) and charge (Figure 2D) of the sEPSCs were comparable between modiolar and pillar SGN boutons (AmpsEPSC –69.37±13.91 pA [n=8 modiolar] vs –87.21±9.49 pA [n=15 pillar]; p=0.2913, unpaired t-test; QsEPSC 63.74±7.77 fC [modiolar] vs 72.54±9.57 fC [pillar]; p=0.5463, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: sEPSC of pillar SGN boutons showed significantly shorter 10–90% rise times than the modiolar ones.
source: sEPSC of pillar SGN boutons showed significantly shorter 10–90% rise times than the modiolar ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C; 0.38±0.04 ms vs 0.57±0.06 ms; p=0.0111, unpaired t-test), yet similar decay times and full-width half-maximum (FWHM, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D–E; p=0.7997 and p=0.9198, respectively, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pillar and modiolar synapses had similar decay times and full-width half-maximum.
source: sEPSC of pillar SGN boutons showed significantly shorter 10–90% rise times than the modiolar ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C; 0.38±0.04 ms vs 0.57±0.06 ms; p=0.0111, unpaired t-test), yet similar decay times and full-width half-maximum (FWHM, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D–E; p=0.7997 and p=0.9198, respectively, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: There was a non-significant trend toward higher percentages of monophasic sEPSCs for pillar synapses.
source: As a second approach to sEPSC properties, we quantified the percentage of monophasic (or temporally more compact) sEPSCs (Chapochnikov et al., 2014; Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002) and found a non-significant trend toward higher percentages of monophasic sEPSCs for pillar synapses (Figure 2G; 25.57 ± 6.9% for modiolar vs 46.65 ± 7.06% for pillar; p=0.0681, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: SR was significantly higher for the pillar synapses compared to modiolar ones.
source: Finally, SR was significantly higher for the pillar synapses (Figure 2I, mean SR of 2.30±0.96 sEPSC/s; median 0.59; n=20) compared to modiolar ones (Figure 2I, mean SR of 0.22±0.09 sEPSC/s; median 0.05; n=13; p=0.0311, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: High SR synapses had significantly larger sEPSCs than low SR synapses.
source: High SR synapses had significantly larger sEPSCs (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1Fi; average sEPSC amplitude of –105.2±8.47 pA for high SR [n=10] vs –62.39±9.67 pA for low SR [n=13]; p=0.0042, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2J.

claim: sEPSC charge tended to be larger in high SR SGN synapses.
source: sEPSC charge tended to be larger in high SR SGN synapses (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1Fii; QsEPSC 84.23±10.38 fC for high SR vs 58.14±7.79 fC for low SR; p=0.0527, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The fraction of monophasic sEPSCs was significantly higher in high SR synapses compared to low SR synapses.
source: The fraction of monophasic sEPSCs was significantly higher in high SR synapses (Figure 2L; 52.08 ± 6.65%; median 43.71%) compared to low SR synapses (29.49 ± 7.43%; median 22.22%; p=0.0185, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: High SR synapses showed significantly faster 10–90% rise times than low SR synapses.
source: High SR synapses also showed a significantly faster 10–90% rise times (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G; 0.36±0.04 ms) than low SR synapses (0.51±0.05 ms; p=0.0420, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Decay time constant and FWHM were not different between low and high SR pairs.
source: Other sEPSCs kinetics, such as decay time constant and FWHM, were not different between low and high SR pairs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and I; p=0.7969 and p=0.9948, respectively, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: 9 out of 10 synapses with SR≥1 sEPSC were located on the pillar side of the IHC.
source: Yet, 9 out of 10 synapses with SR≥1 sEPSC were located on the pillar side of the IHC.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a summary finding.

claim: Mature IHCs of the 'high-frequency' mouse cochlea have graded receptor potentials that primarily represent the rectified envelope of an acoustic stimulus.
source: We used step depolarizations to emulate physiological receptor potentials given that mature IHCs of the 'high-frequency' mouse cochlea have graded receptor potentials that primarily represent the rectified envelope of an acoustic stimulus (i.e. the DC component; Russell and Sellick, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Russell and Sellick, 1978.

claim: IHCs with synapses classified as high or low SR had similar Ca2+ current-voltage relationships.
source: IHCs with synapses classified as high (n=10) or low SR (n=21) had similar Ca2+ current-voltage (IV) relationships: comparable maximal Ca2+ currents (Figure 3Bi; p=0.6939, Mann-Whitney U test) elicited at similar potentials (Figure 3Bii; p=0.1795, unpaired t-test) and comparable reversal potentials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; p=0.4034, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3Bi, Bii, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The voltage dependence of activation of whole-cell Ca2+ influx was similar between IHCs contacted by high and low SR boutons.
source: The voltage dependence of activation of whole-cell Ca2+ influx was similar between IHCs contacted by high and low SR boutons: threshold of Ca2+ influx (Figure 3Ei; p=0.2393, unpaired t-test), Vhalf ICa (Figure 3Fi; p=0.3479, unpaired t-test), and voltage sensitivity of Ca2+ influx (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; p=0.3470, unpaired t-test) did not differ significantly between IHCs contacted by low or high SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3Ei, Fi, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Q50 EPSC of high SR synapses was 6.76±2.0 mV more negative compared to low SR synapses.
source: Q50 EPSC (Figure 3Fii) of high SR synapses (–47.76±1.4 mV; n=10) was 6.76±2.0 mV more negative compared to low SR synapses (–41.00±1.2 mV; n=19; p=0.0021, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3Fii.

claim: High SR synapses had lower voltage thresholds of release than low SR synapses (Q10 EPSC).
source: Accordingly, high SR synapses had lower voltage thresholds of release than low SR synapses (Figure 3Eii, Q10 EPSC of –56.91±1.5 mV [median –56.64 mV] vs –47.39±1.4 mV [median –48.89 mV]; p=0.0001, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3Eii.

claim: The hyperpolarized shift was not significant for Q90 EPSC.
source: The hyperpolarized shift was not significant for Q90 EPSC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; p=0.1706, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The voltage sensitivity of release tended to be lower in high SR than in low SR synapses without reaching statistical significance.
source: The voltage sensitivity of release, determined by a slope factor, tended to be lower in high SR (4.16±0.75 mV) than in low SR (2.9±0.35 mV) synapses without reaching statistical significance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; p=0.0940, unpaired t-test;).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The dynamic range tended to be larger for high SR synapses without reaching significance.
source: The dynamic range, defined as the voltage range for which the exocytosis changes from 10% to 90% (Q90 EPSC – Q10 EPSC), tended to be larger for high SR synapses without reaching significance (Figure 3G; 18.30±3.3 mV for high SR synapses vs 12.78±1.5 mV for low SR synapses; p=0.0940, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The voltage dependence of activation of Ca2+ influx and of SV release did not differ significantly when the synapses were grouped based on their topographical location at the IHC.
source: The voltage dependence of activation of Ca2+ influx and of SV release did not differ significantly when the synapses were grouped based on their topographical location at the IHC (n=12 modiolar synapses vs n=17 pillar synapses; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–K).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–K.

claim: Pillar SR synapses had a tendency to show lower voltage thresholds of release than modiolar synapses.
source: However, pillar SR synapses had a tendency to show lower voltage thresholds of release than modiolar synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Gii; Q10 EPSC of –52.78±1.8 mV [median –53.73 mV] vs –47.68±1.8 mV [median –49.30 mV]; p=0.0725, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Gii.

claim: A supralinear intrinsic Ca2+ dependence of exocytosis in IHCs (Ca2+ cooperativity, m~3–4) has been observed for IHCs of the cochlear apex in mice after hearing onset.
source: We note that a supralinear intrinsic Ca2+ dependence of exocytosis in IHCs (i.e. Ca2+ cooperativity, m~3–4 when changing the single channel current) has been observed for IHCs of the cochlear apex in mice after hearing onset (Brandt et al., 2005; Jaime Tobón and Moser, 2023; Özçete and Moser, 2021; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: A lower Ca2+ cooperativity (m<2) was observed when primarily changing the number of open Ca2+ channels.
source: In contrast, a lower Ca2+ cooperativity was observed in these studies when primarily changing the number of open Ca2+ channels (m<2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies.

claim: Ca2+ cooperativities of m<2 were found for all but 2 synapses.
source: We fitted power functions (QEPSC = a(QCa)m) to the relationships for individual synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and found Ca2+ cooperativities of m<2 for all but 2 synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: High SR synapses had significantly lower Ca2+ cooperativities than low SR synapses.
source: Interestingly, however, high SR synapses, on average, had significantly lower Ca2+ cooperativities than low SR synapses (Figure 3H; mhighSR of 0.8±0.1 [median 0.75; n=10] vs mlowSR of 1.4±0.1 [median 1.37; n=21]; p=0.0016, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The fit to pooled normalized data of high and low SR synapses yielded Ca2+ cooperativities of mhighSR of 0.8 and mlowSR of 1.4.
source: The fit to pooled normalized data of high and low SR synapses yielded the same Ca2+ cooperativities of mhighSR of 0.8 and mlowSR of 1.4 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Pillar synapses showed significantly lower Ca2+ cooperativities than modiolar synapses.
source: When grouped based on their modiolar or pillar location, pillar synapses showed significantly lower Ca2+ cooperativities than modiolar synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L; mpillar of 1.0±0.08 [median 0.88; n=19] vs mmodiolar of 1.6±0.2 [median 1.3; n=12]; p=0.0202, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Most afferent IHC synapses of hearing mice employ a tight, Ca2+ nanodomain-like control of release sites by one or few Ca2+ channel(s) for physiological sound encoding.
source: Our findings indicate that most afferent IHC synapses of hearing mice employ a tight, Ca2+ nanodomain-like control of release sites by one or few Ca2+ channel(s) for physiological sound encoding.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the Ca2+ cooperativity findings.

claim: A control of SV release by ~1 Ca2+ channel prevails at high SR/pillar synapses.
source: Yet, quantitative differences in coupling seem to exist between high SR/pillar synapses and low SR/modiolar synapses, whereby a control of SV release by ~1 Ca2+ channel prevails at high SR/pillar synapses.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the Ca2+ cooperativity data.

claim: In 13 of the 31 paired recordings, a forward masking paradigm was employed to study SV pool dynamics.
source: In 13 of the 31 aforementioned paired recordings (6 classified as low SR and 7 as high SR; 2 belonging to modiolar and 11 to pillar synapses), we employed a forward masking paradigm to study SV pool dynamics of single afferent synapses.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: There was no difference in the peak, initial and final IHC Ca2+ currents and Ca2+ current charge between the recordings from high and low SR synapses.
source: At the presynaptic level, there was no difference in the peak, initial and final IHC Ca2+ currents (ICa) and Ca2+ current charge (QCa) between the recordings from high and low SR synapses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: High SR synapses had significantly shorter synaptic delays than low SR synapses.
source: High SR synapses had significantly shorter synaptic delays (Figure 4B), with mean latencies of the first eEPSC after stimulus onset of 1.17±0.09 ms (median 1.18) compared to 3.34±1.04 ms (median 2.09) in low SR pairs (p=0.0082, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The latency jitter was significantly smaller in high SR synapses compared to low SR synapses.
source: The latency jitter (measured as the standard deviation of the masker-evoked EPSC latencies; Figure 4C) was also significantly smaller in high SR synapses compared to low SR synapses (0.38±0.07 ms [median 0.41] vs 1.67±0.72 ms [median 0.98], respectively; p=0.0012, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High SR synapses had significantly larger peak amplitudes of the masker-evoked EPSCs than low SR synapses.
source: Additionally, high SR synapses had significantly larger peak amplitudes of the masker-evoked EPSCs which reports the initial release from the RRP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; –420.9±54.22 pA for high SR synapses vs –240.1±23.19 pA for low SR synapses; p=0.0149, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The charge of masker-evoked EPSCs was more comparable between high and low SR synapses.
source: In contrast, the charge of masker-evoked EPSCs (QEPSC MASKER) was more comparable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G; 4.512±0.82 pC for high SR vs 3.020±0.43 pC for low SR pairs; p=0.1535, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The quantal content (RRP size in #SV) was comparable between high and low SR synapses.
source: The quantal content (RRP size in #SV) was comparable between high and low SR synapses (Figure 4E, 13.99±2.239 SVs vs 14.28±4.839 SVs, respectively; p=0.9553, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The RRP depleted significantly faster in high SR synapses than in low SR synapses.
source: However, the RRP depleted significantly faster in high SR synapses (Figure 4F): τRRP depletion was 6.347±1.096 ms (median 6.13) for high SR vs 20.88±5.063 ms (median 19.93) for low SR synapses (p=0.0140, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: High SR synapses showed significantly higher initial release rates compared to low SR synapses.
source: Accordingly, high SR synapses showed significantly higher initial release rates compared to low SR synapses (Figure 4G; 2651±660.0 SV/s vs 927.4±307.4 SV/s; p=0.0472, unpaired t-test), which given the comparable RRP size, indicates a higher release probability of the high SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: High SR synapses showed stronger depression of the release rate than low SR synapses.
source: Moreover, high SR synapses showed stronger depression of the release rate (Figure 4I; the ratio of initial/sustained release rate was 5.941±0.916 for high SR pairs and 2.023±0.6251 for low SR pairs; p=0.006, unpaired t-test), despite comparable sustained release rates (Figure 4H; p=0.9258, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Sustained release rates were comparable between high and low SR synapses.
source: Moreover, high SR synapses showed stronger depression of the release rate (Figure 4I; the ratio of initial/sustained release rate was 5.941±0.916 for high SR pairs and 2.023±0.6251 for low SR pairs; p=0.006, unpaired t-test), despite comparable sustained release rates (Figure 4H; p=0.9258, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: All the synapses exhibited a smaller response to the probe compared to the response to the masker stimulus.
source: All the synapses exhibited a smaller response (Figure 4J) and a longer response latency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) to the probe compared to the response to the masker stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: All the synapses exhibited a longer response latency to the probe compared to the response to the masker stimulus.
source: All the synapses exhibited a smaller response (Figure 4J) and a longer response latency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) to the probe compared to the response to the masker stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Short-term synaptic depression probably reflects RRP depletion by the masker stimulus.
source: This short-term synaptic depression probably reflects RRP depletion by the masker stimulus (Avissar et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2011; Frank et al., 2010; Moser and Beutner, 2000), in contrast to previous reports of synaptic facilitation when employing short paired stimuli from more hyperpolarized resting potential that do not trigger the full RRP release (Chen and von Gersdorff, 2019; Goutman and Glowatzki, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: Approximately half of the synapses showed a lower ratio at 16 ms than at 4 ms regardless of their SR.
source: Surprisingly, and contrary to a previous report in auditory bullfrog synapses (Cho et al., 2011), approximately half of the synapses showed a lower ratio at 16 ms than at 4 ms regardless of their SR.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to Cho et al., 2011.

claim: There was no significant difference in the time constant of RRP recovery between high SR and low SR synapses.
source: We did not find a significant difference between high SR and low SR synapses (Figure 4K; τrecovery RRP: 451.5±187.0 ms [median 192.7] vs 2416±2064 ms [median 157.9], respectively; p=0.5338, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The time to the first sEPSC after probe offset took longer in high SR synapses compared to low ones.
source: In 4 high SR and 4 low SR synapses, spontaneous activity was resumed shortly after the offset of the probe. The time to this first sEPSC took longer in high SR synapses compared to low ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M ; 185.2±25.25 ms [median 161.6] vs 104.5±24.10 ms [median 108.4], respectively; p=0.0286, Mann-Whitney U test), again indicating stronger synaptic depression on high SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M.

claim: About 90% of high SR synapses were located at the pillar side of the IHC.
source: We found that about 90% of high SR synapses were located at the pillar side of the IHC.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: RRP size was comparable between high and low SR synapses.
source: RRP size, rate of sustained exocytosis, and kinetics of RRP recovery from depletion were comparable between high and low SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Rate of sustained exocytosis was comparable between high and low SR synapses.
source: RRP size, rate of sustained exocytosis, and kinetics of RRP recovery from depletion were comparable between high and low SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Kinetics of RRP recovery from depletion were comparable between high and low SR synapses.
source: RRP size, rate of sustained exocytosis, and kinetics of RRP recovery from depletion were comparable between high and low SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: High SR synapses exhibit higher release probability which likely reflects the tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and release sites.
source: We conclude that high SR synapses exhibit higher release probability which likely reflects the tighter coupling of Ca2+ channels and release sites.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Diversity in the response properties of individual synapses most likely expands the capacity of a single IHC to encode sound intensity over the wide range of audible sound pressures.
source: This diversity in the response properties of individual synapses most likely expands the capacity of a single IHC to encode sound intensity over the wide range of audible sound pressures.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: The SR range observed in paired recordings from mouse afferent synapses (0–18 sEPSC/s) agrees with results obtained without patch-clamping the IHC (0–16 sEPSC/s).
source: The SR range observed in our paired recordings from mouse afferent synapses (0–18 sEPSC/s) agrees with results obtained without patch-clamping the IHC (0–16 sEPSC/s) and with previous ex vivo reports using loose patch recordings from SGNs of p15–17 rats (0.1–16.42 spikes/s; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: The SR range observed in paired recordings agrees with previous ex vivo reports using loose patch recordings from SGNs of p15–17 rats (0.1–16.42 spikes/s).
source: The SR range observed in our paired recordings from mouse afferent synapses (0–18 sEPSC/s) agrees with results obtained without patch-clamping the IHC (0–16 sEPSC/s) and with previous ex vivo reports using loose patch recordings from SGNs of p15–17 rats (0.1–16.42 spikes/s; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: The maximum rate observed ex vivo is considerably smaller than those recorded in vivo from single SGNs of p14–15 mice (up to 60 spikes/s).
source: However, the maximum rate is considerably smaller than those recorded in vivo from single SGNs of p14–15 mice (up to 60 spikes/s; Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Wong et al., 2013.

claim: In vivo, the IHC resting potential might be more depolarized and/or subject to spontaneous fluctuations that can trigger Ca2+ channel openings and release.
source: This threefold difference between ex vivo and in vivo recordings of the same age group could indicate that, in vivo, the IHC resting potential might be more depolarized and/or subject to spontaneous fluctuations that can trigger Ca2+ channel openings and release.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the difference between ex vivo and in vivo recordings.

claim: The presence of K+ channel blockers (TEA and Cs+) and differences in pH could have an impact on the excitability of the cell and the kinetics of the cellular processes.
source: Additionally, the presence of K+ channel blockers (tetraethylammonium [TEA] and Cs+) and differences in pH could all have an impact on the excitability of the cell and the kinetics of the cellular processes.
evidence: This is stated as a possible factor affecting the results.

claim: The intrinsic biophysical properties of SGNs could further expand the firing rate distribution.
source: Other important factors might explain the higher SR reported in vivo: (i) The intrinsic biophysical properties of SGNs which could further expand the firing rate distribution (Markowitz and Kalluri, 2020), for instance, due to spikes initiated intrinsically and not activated by an EPSP (Wu et al., 2016);
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with citations.

claim: There may be a sampling bias of synapses with SR above 20 sEPSC/s given that they constitute less than 35% of SGNs from 8- to 17-week-old mice.
source: (ii) a sampling bias of synapses with SR above 20 sEPSC/s given that they constitute less than 35% of SGNs from 8- to 17-week-old mice (Taberner and Liberman, 2005);
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with citation to Taberner and Liberman, 2005.

claim: There is developmental recruitment of high SR SGNs with age.
source: and (iii) the developmental recruitment of high SR SGNs with age (Niwa et al., 2021; Romand, 1984; Walsh and McGee, 1987; Wong et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: 90% of the paired recordings were obtained from mice between p14 and p17.
source: 90% of the paired recordings (and 60% for the bouton recordings) of our dataset were obtained from mice between p14 and p17, in which spontaneous activity is still low compared to older age groups (p19–21: 0–44.22 spikes/s; p29–32: 0.11–54.9 spikes/s [Wu et al., 2016]; p28: 0–47.94 spikes/s [Siebald et al., 2023]).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citations.

claim: Type Ib and Ic SGNs preferentially synapse on the modiolar side.
source: For instance, type Ib and Ic SGNs preferentially synapse on the modiolar side (Sherrill et al., 2019; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018) and show low SR (Siebald et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Type Ib and Ic SGNs show low SR.
source: For instance, type Ib and Ic SGNs preferentially synapse on the modiolar side (Sherrill et al., 2019; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018) and show low SR (Siebald et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Siebald et al., 2023.

claim: Pillar synapses are preferentially formed by type Ia SGNs.
source: Pillar synapses are preferentially formed by type Ia SGNs (Shrestha et al., 2018; Siebald et al., 2023), have smaller IHC active zones (AZs) (Liberman et al., 2011; Ohn et al., 2016; Reijntjes et al., 2020), and activate at voltages as low as the IHC resting potential (Ohn et al., 2016; Özçete and Moser, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Pillar synapses have smaller IHC active zones.
source: Pillar synapses are preferentially formed by type Ia SGNs (Shrestha et al., 2018; Siebald et al., 2023), have smaller IHC active zones (AZs) (Liberman et al., 2011; Ohn et al., 2016; Reijntjes et al., 2020), and activate at voltages as low as the IHC resting potential (Ohn et al., 2016; Özçete and Moser, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Pillar synapses activate at voltages as low as the IHC resting potential.
source: Pillar synapses are preferentially formed by type Ia SGNs (Shrestha et al., 2018; Siebald et al., 2023), have smaller IHC active zones (AZs) (Liberman et al., 2011; Ohn et al., 2016; Reijntjes et al., 2020), and activate at voltages as low as the IHC resting potential (Ohn et al., 2016; Özçete and Moser, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The low voltage of activation of release at pillar synapses shown ex vivo could underly the high SR and low sound threshold of firing of SGNs found in vivo.
source: The low voltage of activation of release at pillar synapses shown ex vivo could underly the high SR and low sound threshold of firing of SGNs found in vivo but direct demonstration of such a link has been missing.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis that the current study aims to test.

claim: Not all the synapses of the pillar IHC side had high SR.
source: Yet, not all the synapses of the pillar IHC side had high SR, which agrees with a recent study of molecularly tagged SGNs (Siebald et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Siebald et al., 2023.

claim: High-frequency and large-amplitude sEPSCs occur predominantly in synapses with smaller ribbons and AZs.
source: These findings suggest that high-frequency and large-amplitude sEPSCs occur predominantly in synapses with smaller ribbons and AZs, opposing results from retinal cells in which smaller ribbons resulted in reduced frequency and amplitude of EPSCs (Mehta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citation to Mehta et al., 2013.

claim: Other studies support an overall pillar-modiolar gradient with 'salt and pepper' intermingling of synaptic properties rather than their strict segregation.
source: Moreover, other studies also support an overall pillar-modiolar gradient with 'salt and pepper' intermingling of synaptic properties rather than their strict segregation (Ohn et al., 2016; Özçete and Moser, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: High variability in the waveform and amplitude of sEPSCs between synapses has been found in previous reports.
source: Similar to previous reports (e.g. Chapochnikov et al., 2014; Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002; Grant et al., 2010; Huang and Moser, 2018; Rutherford et al., 2012), we found a high variability in the waveform and amplitude of sEPSCs between synapses, which apparently do not strictly depend on the topographical location of the synapse (the present work and Niwa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: The difference in the percentage of monophasic sEPSCs and rise times in low and high SR synapses could arise from variability in the fusion pore dynamics.
source: The difference in the percentage of monophasic sEPSCs and rise times in low and high SR synapses could arise from variability in the fusion pore dynamics on the way to SV fusion and/or on the number of SVs released in timely manner.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation.

claim: In the view of the multivesicular hypothesis of spontaneous release, SVs of a modiolar AZ might fuse in an uncoordinated manner, creating EPSCs with a less compact waveform and slower rise times.
source: In the view of the multivesicular hypothesis of spontaneous release (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002; Li et al., 2009; Niwa et al., 2021; Schnee et al., 2013), SVs of a modiolar AZ might fuse in an uncoordinated manner, creating EPSCs with a less compact waveform and slower rise times.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations.

claim: Each sEPSC corresponds to a unitary release event ('univesicular mode of release').
source: Alternatively and our favorite hypothesis, each sEPSC corresponds to a unitary release event ('univesicular mode of release'; Chapochnikov et al., 2014; Grabner and Moser, 2018; Huang and Moser, 2018; Young et al., 2021) that has the capacity to drive action potential firing (Rutherford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as the authors' preferred hypothesis with citations.

claim: In the framework of the univesicular hypothesis, the flickering of the fusion pore might be favored in low SR synapses, leading to slower sEPSC rise times and a lower percentage of monophasic sEPSCs.
source: In the framework of the univesicular hypothesis of spontaneous release, the flickering of the fusion pore, prior to or instead of full collapse fusion of the SV, might be favored in low SR synapses, leading to slower sEPSC rise times and a lower percentage of monophasic sEPSCs.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation within the univesicular hypothesis framework.

claim: Heterogeneity of fusion pore dynamics has been reported in chromaffin cells, calyx of Held, and hippocampal neurons.
source: Such heterogeneity of fusion pore dynamics has been reported in chromaffin cells, calyx of Held, and hippocampal neurons (Chang et al., 2021; Henkel et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: sEPSC amplitudes of IHC synapses in hearing mice seem lower than in previous ex vivo studies on IHC synapses of hearing rats.
source: Finally, we note that sEPSC amplitudes of IHC synapses in hearing mice (present study and Niwa et al., 2021) seem lower than in previous ex vivo studies on IHC synapses of hearing rats (Chapochnikov et al., 2014; Grant et al., 2010; Huang and Moser, 2018; Young et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: In rats, the EPSC amplitude distribution changes with maturation, from highly skewed to the left with a peak around –30 pA to a Gaussian-like distribution with a peak at –375 pA.
source: In rats, the EPSC amplitude distribution changes with maturation, from highly skewed to the left with a peak around –30 pA to a Gaussian-like distribution with a peak at –375 pA (Grant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Grant et al., 2010.

claim: This developmental change in EPSC amplitude distribution does not seem to be the case in mouse IHC synapses.
source: This does not seem to be the case in mouse IHC synapses.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing mouse and rat data.

claim: Average EPSC amplitudes in pre-hearing mice are around –100 to –150 pA.
source: Average EPSC amplitudes in pre-hearing mice are around –100 to –150 pA (Chapochnikov et al., 2014), even with 40 mM K+ stimulation (Jing et al., 2013; Takago et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Mean EPSC amplitudes in hearing mice remained small (around –100 pA) in resting conditions.
source: On the contrary, mean EPSC amplitudes in hearing mice remained small (around –100 pA) in resting conditions (Niwa et al., 2021 and the present study), but became significantly larger upon stimulation with 40 mM K+ (Niwa et al., 2021) or voltage depolarizations (the present study, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: High SR synapses showed lower voltage thresholds of synaptic transmission, resembling in vivo evoked firing properties of high SR SGNs.
source: In an intriguing resemblance with in vivo evoked firing properties of high SR SGNs (Bourien et al., 2014; Buran et al., 2010; Relkin and Doucet, 1991; Rhode and Smith, 1985; Taberner and Liberman, 2005), high SR synapses showed lower voltage (~sound pressure in vivo) thresholds of synaptic transmission (~firing in vivo), shorter and less variable synaptic latencies (~first spike latencies in vivo), and higher initial release rates (~onset firing rate in vivo).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations comparing ex vivo and in vivo findings.

claim: High SR synapses showed shorter and less variable synaptic latencies, resembling in vivo evoked firing properties of high SR SGNs.
source: In an intriguing resemblance with in vivo evoked firing properties of high SR SGNs (Bourien et al., 2014; Buran et al., 2010; Relkin and Doucet, 1991; Rhode and Smith, 1985; Taberner and Liberman, 2005), high SR synapses showed lower voltage (~sound pressure in vivo) thresholds of synaptic transmission (~firing in vivo), shorter and less variable synaptic latencies (~first spike latencies in vivo), and higher initial release rates (~onset firing rate in vivo).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations comparing ex vivo and in vivo findings.

claim: High SR synapses showed higher initial release rates, resembling in vivo evoked firing properties of high SR SGNs.
source: In an intriguing resemblance with in vivo evoked firing properties of high SR SGNs (Bourien et al., 2014; Buran et al., 2010; Relkin and Doucet, 1991; Rhode and Smith, 1985; Taberner and Liberman, 2005), high SR synapses showed lower voltage (~sound pressure in vivo) thresholds of synaptic transmission (~firing in vivo), shorter and less variable synaptic latencies (~first spike latencies in vivo), and higher initial release rates (~onset firing rate in vivo).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations comparing ex vivo and in vivo findings.

claim: Stronger synaptic depression at high SR synapses agrees well with the finding of a greater ratio of peak to adapted firing rate in high SR SGNs recorded in vivo.
source: In addition, we found stronger synaptic depression at high SR synapses, which agrees well with the finding of a greater ratio of peak to adapted firing rate in high SR SGNs recorded in vivo (Taberner and Liberman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Taberner and Liberman, 2005.

claim: In high SR synapses, a more hyperpolarized Ca2+ channel activation in combination with tighter coupling between the Ca2+ channels and the Ca2+ sensor of fusion would enable a faster response with a greater initial SV release probability.
source: Our hypothesis is that, in high SR synapses, a more hyperpolarized Ca2+ channel activation (Ohn et al., 2016) in combination with tighter coupling between the Ca2+ channels and the Ca2+ sensor of fusion (this work and Özçete and Moser, 2021) would enable a faster response with a greater initial SV release probability for a given stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' hypothesis with citations.

claim: The spatial coupling of the Ca2+ channel to the SV release site has been shown to greatly affect release probability in other synapses.
source: The spatial coupling of the Ca2+ channel to the SV release site has also been shown to greatly affect release probability in other synapses (Eggermann et al., 2011; Fekete et al., 2019; Moser et al., 2020; Rebola et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: A heterogenous Ca2+ coupling would diversify the response properties of individual synapses to the same stimulus.
source: Thus, a heterogenous Ca2+ coupling would diversify the response properties (i.e. SV release probability) of individual synapses to the same stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation.

claim: Genetic disruptions that shifted the voltage dependence had a greater impact on the in vivo distribution of SR and onset firing rate of SGNs than mutations that changed the maximal synaptic Ca2+ influx.
source: Interestingly, genetic disruptions that shifted the voltage dependence had a greater impact on the in vivo distribution of SR and onset firing rate of SGNs than mutations that changed the maximal synaptic Ca2+ influx (Jean et al., 2018; Ohn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Paired pre- and postsynaptic patch-clamp recordings and single synapse imaging jointly found a lower apparent Ca2+ cooperativity in pillar synapses.
source: Paired pre- and postsynaptic patch-clamp recordings (this work) and single synapse imaging of presynaptic Ca2+ signals and glutamate release (Özçete and Moser, 2021) jointly found a lower apparent Ca2+ cooperativity in pillar synapses during depolarizations within the range of receptor potentials.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Özçete and Moser, 2021.

claim: Single synapse imaging found a wider range of apparent Ca2+ cooperativities than paired patch-clamp recordings.
source: However, single synapse imaging (Özçete and Moser, 2021) found a wider range of apparent Ca2+ cooperativities than our two non-overlapping datasets for paired patch-clamp recordings (this work and Jaime Tobón and Moser, 2023).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Single synapse imaging assessed the presynaptic Ca2+ influx of the specific synapse, while in paired recordings the release was related to the whole-cell Ca2+ influx.
source: This might reflect two important technical differences: (i) single synapse imaging assessed the presynaptic Ca2+ influx of the specific synapse, while in paired recordings we related release to the whole-cell Ca2+ influx, and (ii) the temporal resolution of paired recordings allowed to study the initial release rate using shorter stimuli than in imaging, which avoids an impact of RRP depletion and ongoing SV replenishment.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the difference between imaging and paired recording results.

claim: The temporal resolution of paired recordings allowed to study the initial release rate using shorter stimuli than in imaging, which avoids an impact of RRP depletion and ongoing SV replenishment.
source: This might reflect two important technical differences: (i) single synapse imaging assessed the presynaptic Ca2+ influx of the specific synapse, while in paired recordings we related release to the whole-cell Ca2+ influx, and (ii) the temporal resolution of paired recordings allowed to study the initial release rate using shorter stimuli than in imaging, which avoids an impact of RRP depletion and ongoing SV replenishment.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the difference between imaging and paired recording results.

claim: Other factors that affect release probability include variations in the number of open Ca2+ channels at the AZ.
source: Other factors that affect release probability include variations in the number of open Ca2+ channels at the AZ (Gratz et al., 2019; Holderith et al., 2012; Scimemi and Diamond, 2012; Sheng et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2013) and the fusion competence of the SV (Klenchin and Martin, 2000), including the priming and docking state (Lin et al., 2022; Neher and Brose, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Other factors that affect release probability include the fusion competence of the SV, including the priming and docking state.
source: Other factors that affect release probability include variations in the number of open Ca2+ channels at the AZ (Gratz et al., 2019; Holderith et al., 2012; Scimemi and Diamond, 2012; Sheng et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2013) and the fusion competence of the SV (Klenchin and Martin, 2000), including the priming and docking state (Lin et al., 2022; Neher and Brose, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The ensuing Ca2+ influx in pillar synapses might facilitate Ca2+ channels and priming of SVs.
source: The ensuing Ca2+ influx in pillar synapses might facilitate Ca2+ channels and priming of SVs (Cho and von Gersdorff, 2012; Goutman and Glowatzki, 2011; Goutman and Glowatzki, 2007; Michalski et al., 2017; Moser and Beutner, 2000; Pangršič et al., 2015; Schnee et al., 2011; Spassova et al., 2004) and contribute to the observed results in high SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a possible mechanism with citations.

claim: It is unknown whether modiolar and pillar synapses exhibit different numbers of docked and primed SVs.
source: Regarding the fusion competence of SVs, it is unknown whether modiolar and pillar synapses exhibit different numbers of docked and primed SVs.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Ultrastructural studies that resolve docked and tethered SVs have not addressed the topographical location of the AZ in the murine IHC.
source: To date, ultrastructural studies that resolve docked and tethered SVs have not addressed the topographical location of the AZ in the murine IHC (Chakrabarti et al., 2022; Chakrabarti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The estimated RRP of about 14 SVs in both high and low SR synapses compares well to prior estimates obtained using ex vivo electrophysiology (10–40 SVs).
source: Our estimated RRP of about 14 SVs in both high and low SR synapses compares well to prior estimates obtained using ex vivo electrophysiology (10–40 SVs: Goutman and Glowatzki, 2007; Jean et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2005; Khimich et al., 2005; Moser and Beutner, 2000; Pangrsic et al., 2010; Schnee et al., 2005), model-based analysis of SGN firing (4–40 SVs; Frank et al., 2010; Jean et al., 2018; Peterson et al., 2014), and electron microscopy (10–16 SVs within 50 nm of the presynaptic membrane; Chakrabarti et al., 2018; Frank et al., 2010; Graydon et al., 2011; Kantardzhieva et al., 2013; Khimich et al., 2005; Pangrsic et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Previous reports based on electron microscopy suggested larger pools of SVs at modiolar synapses.
source: However, previous reports based on electron microscopy (Kantardzhieva et al., 2013; Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996; Michanski et al., 2019) suggested larger pools of SVs at modiolar synapses, while our electrophysiological estimate of RRP size was comparable between low and high SR synapses.
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Higher release probability with comparable RRP size explains higher initial release rates.
source: However, higher release probability with comparable RRP size explains higher initial release rates, which likely explain the faster and temporally more precise postsynaptic depolarization that is likely to turn into shorter first spike latencies and lower first spike latency jitter (this study and Buran et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citation to Buran et al., 2010.

claim: The heterogeneity in the functional properties of IHC synapses could arise from molecular heterogeneity of the AZ.
source: Finally, the heterogeneity in the functional properties of IHC synapses could arise from molecular heterogeneity of the AZ.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation.

claim: In central glutamatergic synapses, molecular heterogeneity of synaptic proteins plays a critical role in the modulation of SV release probability and priming state.
source: In central glutamatergic synapses, molecular heterogeneity of synaptic proteins plays a critical role in the modulation of SV release probability and priming state (Neher and Brose, 2018; Wichmann and Kuner, 2022).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Differential isoforms of priming factors and scaffold proteins have been suggested to tune the functional synaptic diversity of central synapses.
source: For instance, differential isoforms of priming factors and scaffold proteins have been suggested to tune the functional synaptic diversity of central synapses (Fulterer et al., 2018; Rebola et al., 2019; Rosenmund et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Cochlear IHCs have an unconventional fusion machinery that appears to work without neuronal SNARES.
source: Cochlear IHCs have an unconventional fusion machinery that appears to work without neuronal SNARES (Nouvian et al., 2011) (but see Calvet et al., 2022) and priming factors such as Munc13 and CAPS (Vogl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Cochlear IHCs appear to work without priming factors such as Munc13 and CAPS.
source: Cochlear IHCs have an unconventional fusion machinery that appears to work without neuronal SNARES (Nouvian et al., 2011) (but see Calvet et al., 2022) and priming factors such as Munc13 and CAPS (Vogl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Vogl et al., 2015.

claim: Promising candidates for molecular heterogeneity include RBPs, RIMs, and Septin.
source: Promising candidates include RBPs (Butola et al., 2021; Grauel et al., 2016; Krinner et al., 2021; Krinner et al., 2017; Petzoldt et al., 2020), RIMs (Jung et al., 2015; Picher et al., 2017b), and Septin (Fekete et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Parameters such as RRP size, sustained exocytosis, and recovery of spontaneous and evoked release did not differ among high and low SR synapses.
source: Parameters such as RRP size (~# spikes of the rapidly adapting component of firing), sustained exocytosis (~adapted firing rate in vivo), recovery of spontaneous and evoked release (~recovery from forward masking in vivo) did not differ among our high and low SR synapses, and contrasts with in vivo data (e.g. Bourien et al., 2014; Buran et al., 2010; Relkin and Doucet, 1991; Rhode and Smith, 1985; Taberner and Liberman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: High SR synapses tended to show broader dynamic ranges with shallower slopes, while in vivo, high SR SGNs show smaller dynamic ranges and steeper slopes than the low SR ones.
source: High SR synapses tended to show broader dynamic ranges with shallower slopes, while, in vivo, high SR SGNs show smaller dynamic ranges and steeper slopes than the low SR ones (Ohlemiller et al., 1991; Winter et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The non-linear saturating properties of the basilar membrane might widen the rate level function of low SR SGNs.
source: Could this reflect the non-linear saturating properties of the basilar membrane (Sachs et al., 1989; Sachs and Abbas, 1974; Yates et al., 1990) (discussed in Ohlemiller et al., 1991) which might widen the rate level function of low SR SGNs?
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with citations.

claim: Partial depletion of the 'standing' RRP at high SR synapses in vivo might explain differences between ex vivo and in vivo findings.
source: Or is it due to a partial depletion of the 'standing' RRP (i.e. the occupancy of the RRP release sites with a fusion-competent SV; Moser, 2020; Pangrsic et al., 2010) at high SR synapses in vivo?
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with citations.

claim: Possible mechanisms downstream of glutamate release and AMPA receptor activation include different spike rates due to diverse EPSC waveforms.
source: The possible mechanisms include but are not limited to: (i) different spike rates due to diverse EPSC waveforms (Rutherford et al., 2012); (ii) differences in SGN excitability (Crozier and Davis, 2014; Markowitz and Kalluri, 2020; Smith et al., 2015) due to heterogenous molecular (Petitpré et al., 2020; Petitpré et al., 2018; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018) and morphological profiles (Liberman, 1980; Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996; Tsuji and Liberman, 1997); and (iii) differences in efferent innervation of SGNs (Hua et al., 2021; Liberman, 1990; Ruel et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Possible mechanisms downstream of glutamate release and AMPA receptor activation include differences in SGN excitability due to heterogenous molecular and morphological profiles.
source: The possible mechanisms include but are not limited to: (i) different spike rates due to diverse EPSC waveforms (Rutherford et al., 2012); (ii) differences in SGN excitability (Crozier and Davis, 2014; Markowitz and Kalluri, 2020; Smith et al., 2015) due to heterogenous molecular (Petitpré et al., 2020; Petitpré et al., 2018; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018) and morphological profiles (Liberman, 1980; Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996; Tsuji and Liberman, 1997); and (iii) differences in efferent innervation of SGNs (Hua et al., 2021; Liberman, 1990; Ruel et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Possible mechanisms downstream of glutamate release and AMPA receptor activation include differences in efferent innervation of SGNs.
source: The possible mechanisms include but are not limited to: (i) different spike rates due to diverse EPSC waveforms (Rutherford et al., 2012); (ii) differences in SGN excitability (Crozier and Davis, 2014; Markowitz and Kalluri, 2020; Smith et al., 2015) due to heterogenous molecular (Petitpré et al., 2020; Petitpré et al., 2018; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018) and morphological profiles (Liberman, 1980; Merchan-Perez and Liberman, 1996; Tsuji and Liberman, 1997); and (iii) differences in efferent innervation of SGNs (Hua et al., 2021; Liberman, 1990; Ruel et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Caution is to be applied for the comparison of ex vivo and in vivo data due to the partial disruption of the physiological milieu.
